title: Network Policies
summary: By default, Kubernetes allows all pods to communicate with all other pods — a flat network with no isolation. Network Policies are pod-level firewalls that restrict which pods can send or receive traffic and on which ports. Without them, a compromised pod has full lateral movement to every database, API, and service in your cluster.

sections.title: The default open network and why it's dangerous
sections.body:
## The Kubernetes flat network and why default-allow is a security problem

Kubernetes networking is built on a fundamental assumption: **every pod must be able to reach every other pod**, regardless of namespace, without any configuration. This "flat network" model is a deliberate design choice that makes service discovery simple — pods communicate by name via DNS, and no firewall rules need to be configured for basic connectivity. The downside is that it provides zero network-level isolation by default.

In a traditional data centre or cloud deployment, you would place your database servers in a private subnet, your application servers in a semi-public subnet, and your load balancers in a public subnet — with security groups or ACLs enforcing that the database is only reachable from the application tier. In a default Kubernetes cluster, none of this isolation exists. A pod in the `frontend` namespace can open a TCP connection directly to the PostgreSQL service in the `database` namespace. A pod in a shared development namespace can reach the production API.

This matters because **lateral movement** is how most serious breaches unfold. An attacker who compromises a frontend pod via an XSS vulnerability or a dependency CVE will immediately attempt to reach other services: the database (to exfiltrate data), the Kubernetes API server (to read Secrets or deploy backdoors), and internal services that are not exposed externally. In a default-allow network, there is nothing to stop them.

**NetworkPolicy** objects are Kubernetes's answer: they are pod-level firewall rules, expressed as Kubernetes resources, that specify exactly which traffic is allowed. The enforcement is handled by the **CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin** — not all CNIs support NetworkPolicy, so the first operational concern when adding policies to a cluster is confirming that the CNI (Calico, Cilium, Weave, Antrea) actually enforces them.

The key conceptual shift is from a default-allow model to a **default-deny with explicit allow** model — the same principle that underlies every well-designed firewall.

**Kubernetes default: everything talks to everything.**

```bash
# In a default cluster, any pod can reach any other pod:
# Pod A (namespace: default) → can call Pod B (namespace: database)
# Pod B → can call the Kubernetes API server
# Compromised pod → can port-scan the cluster, reach secrets, databases
```

**Why this matters:**

```
Without Network Policies:
  If an attacker compromises a frontend pod, they can:
    1. Call your database service directly (not just via the app)
    2. Exfiltrate data to external IPs
    3. Call the internal Kubernetes API to read Secrets
    4. Move laterally to backend services not exposed externally

With Network Policies (zero-trust):
  frontend pod → can only reach backend pod on port 8080
  backend pod  → can only reach postgres on port 5432
  postgres pod → cannot initiate outbound connections at all
  Any other traffic → DROP
```

**Network Policies are enforced by the CNI plugin:**

```
Not all CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy!

Supports NetworkPolicy:
  Calico     — most feature-rich, supports global policies
  Cilium     — eBPF-based, high performance, Layer 7 support
  Weave      — simple setup
  Antrea     — VMware's CNI

Does NOT support NetworkPolicy:
  Flannel    — must pair with Calico for policy enforcement
  kubenet    — basic CNI (used in some cloud setups)

k3s default: Flannel (no NetworkPolicy support out of the box)
k3s with --cni=calico or --cni=cilium: full support

Note: in this sandbox, NetworkPolicies can be created but may not be
enforced depending on the k3s CNI configuration.
```

**A NetworkPolicy only applies to pods it selects:**

```
If no NetworkPolicy selects a pod → allow all (default behavior preserved)
If any NetworkPolicy selects a pod → that pod is isolated for that direction
  (ingress isolation if the policy has ingress rules,
   egress isolation if the policy has egress rules)

This means: adding a NetworkPolicy is additive — you whitelist.
There is no way to "deny" via NetworkPolicy; you only whitelist allowed traffic.
Everything else is denied once any policy selects the pod.
```

sections.title: NetworkPolicy anatomy: selectors and rules
sections.body:
## Dissecting a NetworkPolicy: selectors, directions, and the AND/OR subtlety

A NetworkPolicy has three core components: a **pod selector** that determines which pods the policy applies to, **policy types** that declare which traffic directions are controlled, and **ingress and egress rules** that specify what traffic is allowed.

The pod selector works the same way as in Deployments and Services — it matches pods by label. An empty `podSelector: {}` selects *all* pods in the namespace. This is how you implement a default-deny policy: select all pods and declare that Ingress and Egress are controlled, but provide no rules — the result is that all traffic to and from those pods is dropped.

A critical property of NetworkPolicy is that it is **additive and whitelist-only**. There is no "deny" rule. Once any NetworkPolicy selects a pod for a given direction (Ingress or Egress), that direction is isolated — only traffic explicitly matched by a rule is allowed. Multiple policies that select the same pod are combined with OR logic: if any policy allows the traffic, it passes.

The **from/to selectors** have a subtle AND/OR distinction that is one of the most common sources of NetworkPolicy bugs. A single item in the `from` array that contains both `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` as fields requires *both* to match (AND logic) — the traffic must come from a pod that is in the matching namespace AND has the matching label. Two separate items in the `from` array are OR conditions — traffic is allowed if it matches either one.

**Egress DNS** is the most commonly forgotten rule. A default-deny policy blocks all outbound traffic, including DNS queries on port 53/UDP. Without an explicit egress rule allowing UDP 53 to the `kube-system` namespace (where kube-dns runs), pods cannot resolve any hostname — not even internal service names. Always add a DNS egress rule when applying default-deny policies.

**Basic structure:**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: my-policy
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:        # which pods this policy applies to
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:        # which direction(s) this policy controls
  - Ingress           # control incoming traffic to selected pods
  - Egress            # control outgoing traffic from selected pods
  ingress:
  - from:             # allow traffic FROM these sources
    - podSelector:    # from pods with this label in same namespace
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:            # on these ports
    - port: 8080
      protocol: TCP
  egress:
  - to:               # allow traffic TO these destinations
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - port: 5432
```

**podSelector — which pods this policy applies to:**

```yaml
podSelector: {}              # empty = select ALL pods in namespace
podSelector:                 # specific pods by label
  matchLabels:
    app: api-server
podSelector:
  matchExpressions:          # more complex selection
  - key: tier
    operator: In
    values: ["frontend", "backend"]
```

**from/to selectors — filter traffic sources/destinations:**

```yaml
from:
# Option 1: pods in same namespace
- podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: monitoring

# Option 2: pods in a specific namespace
- namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      name: monitoring

# Option 3: specific namespace AND specific pods (AND logic)
- namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      name: monitoring
  podSelector:                  # same list item = AND
    matchLabels:
      app: prometheus

# Option 4: either namespace OR pods (OR logic)
- namespaceSelector:            # separate list items = OR
    matchLabels:
      name: monitoring
- podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: prometheus

# Option 5: specific external IP ranges
- ipBlock:
    cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
    except:
    - 10.0.1.0/24             # exclude this subnet
```

**DNS egress — easy to forget:**

```yaml
# Without this, pods can't resolve hostnames!
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector:        # allow DNS queries to kube-dns
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
  ports:
  - port: 53
    protocol: UDP
  - port: 53
    protocol: TCP
```

sections.title: Common Network Policy patterns
sections.body:
## Standard NetworkPolicy patterns for production cluster segmentation

Real-world network segmentation is implemented through a small set of composable patterns. Rather than trying to write one complex policy per application, the standard approach is to layer these patterns: start with a namespace-wide default deny, then add targeted allow rules for each communication path.

The **default-deny** pattern is always the starting point. It uses an empty pod selector (selecting all pods) with both Ingress and Egress in `policyTypes` but no rules — meaning everything is blocked. Once this is in place, every communication path that needs to exist must be explicitly opened.

The **tier-to-tier allow** pattern creates a directed graph of allowed communication paths: frontend → backend on port 8080, backend → database on port 5432. Each policy is scoped to the destination (the pod that receives traffic) and specifies the source (the pod that sends traffic) using pod label selectors. This mirrors the access control model of cloud security groups.

The **cross-namespace monitoring** pattern is common in clusters that run Prometheus in a dedicated `monitoring` namespace. The monitoring pods need to reach the `/metrics` endpoint of pods in all other namespaces. Rather than labelling every pod individually, the pattern uses a `namespaceSelector` that matches the monitoring namespace as the traffic source, combined with a `podSelector: {}` (all pods) as the target.

The **egress-to-external** pattern handles outbound traffic to services outside the cluster — an external API, a cloud storage endpoint, or a managed database. The `ipBlock` selector specifies a CIDR range; the optional `except` field excludes specific sub-ranges (useful for blocking access to the cluster's internal CIDR while allowing the broader internet).

Understanding how to combine these patterns — and remembering to always include DNS egress — lets you implement zero-trust network segmentation for any application topology.

**Pattern 1: Default deny all**

```yaml
# Apply to a namespace first, then whitelist specific traffic.
# The empty podSelector selects ALL pods; no ingress/egress = deny all.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}   # all pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  # No ingress or egress rules = deny everything
```

**Pattern 2: Allow only frontend → backend traffic**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: backend-ingress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - port: 8080
      protocol: TCP
```

**Pattern 3: Namespace isolation (only allow traffic within namespace)**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: namespace-isolation
  namespace: staging
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: staging  # same namespace only
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: staging
  - to:  # also allow DNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
```

**Pattern 4: Allow monitoring namespace to scrape metrics**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-prometheus-scrape
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}  # all pods in production
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
    ports:
    - port: 9090   # metrics endpoint
      protocol: TCP
```

**Pattern 5: Egress to specific external service only**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-egress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-server
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:    # internal postgres
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - port: 5432
  - to:
    - ipBlock:         # external S3
        cidr: 52.216.0.0/14  # AWS S3 IP range (example)
    ports:
    - port: 443
  - to:  # DNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
```

sections.title: Exercise: create and inspect Network Policies
sections.body:
## Hands-on: writing and inspecting NetworkPolicies

This exercise focuses on the most important skills for working with NetworkPolicy in production: writing policies with the correct selector structure, understanding how multiple policies interact, and diagnosing why traffic is blocked or allowed.

Because this sandbox uses k3s with Flannel as the CNI (which does not enforce NetworkPolicy by default), the policies you create will be stored in Kubernetes and syntactically valid — but may not be enforced at the network level. This is actually a useful teaching scenario: it mirrors what happens when you apply policies to a cluster that lacks a policy-enforcing CNI, which is a real operational hazard. Always confirm CNI capability before relying on NetworkPolicies for security.

The Python visualization at step 7 is a practice tool for the kind of reasoning you need when auditing network policies: given a set of policies, which pods can reach which other pods, and on which ports? In a complex production cluster, tools like the Cilium Network Policy editor or kubectl plugins like `np-viewer` automate this analysis.

Pay particular attention to the namespace label prerequisite in step 1. The `namespaceSelector` in NetworkPolicy matches namespace **labels**, not names — and namespaces do not have a `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label by default in older clusters (it was added automatically in Kubernetes 1.21+). Verifying that namespaces have the labels you expect is step one in debugging a `namespaceSelector` that doesn't seem to match.

```bash
# ── 1. Label the namespaces (required for namespaceSelector) ──────────────
kubectl label namespace default kubernetes.io/metadata.name=default --overwrite
kubectl label namespace learning kubernetes.io/metadata.name=learning --overwrite
kubectl label namespace monitoring kubernetes.io/metadata.name=monitoring --overwrite

# ── 2. Create a deny-all policy for the learning namespace ────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: learning
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
EOF

# ── 3. Create the three-tier app labels ──────────────────────────────────
# Label existing pods (we'll use the api-server deployment)
kubectl label deployment api-server -n learning tier=backend

# ── 4. Allow monitoring to scrape the backend ─────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-monitoring-scrape
  namespace: learning
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      tier: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
    ports:
    - port: 9090
      protocol: TCP
    - port: 8080
      protocol: TCP
EOF

# ── 5. Allow DNS egress (required for any real workload) ──────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: learning
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
    - port: 53
      protocol: TCP
EOF

# ── 6. Inspect what we created ────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get networkpolicies -n learning
kubectl describe networkpolicy default-deny-all -n learning
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-monitoring-scrape -n learning

# ── 7. Visualize the policy structure ────────────────────────────────────
python3 << 'PYEOF'
policies = [
    {"name": "default-deny-all",         "selects": "all pods", "ingress": "DENY ALL", "egress": "DENY ALL"},
    {"name": "allow-monitoring-scrape",   "selects": "tier=backend", "ingress": "FROM monitoring ns :9090,:8080", "egress": "-"},
    {"name": "allow-dns-egress",          "selects": "all pods", "ingress": "-", "egress": "TO kube-system :53/UDP"},
]

print(f"{'Policy':<30} {'Selects':<20} {'Ingress':<35} {'Egress'}")
print("-" * 100)
for p in policies:
    print(f"{p['name']:<30} {p['selects']:<20} {p['ingress']:<35} {p['egress']}")
PYEOF

# ── 8. Write a network policy for the default namespace ───────────────────
# Challenge: write a policy that allows:
#   - web-app pods to receive traffic from any pod in default namespace
#   - web-app pods to make outbound calls to the learning namespace on port 8080
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-app-policy
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: default
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: learning
    ports:
    - port: 8080
  - to:  # DNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
EOF

kubectl get networkpolicies -n default
kubectl get networkpolicies -n learning

# ── 9. Clean up ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete networkpolicy default-deny-all allow-monitoring-scrape allow-dns-egress -n learning
kubectl delete networkpolicy web-app-policy -n default 2>/dev/null || true
```

questions.q: A pod has a NetworkPolicy that only has policyTypes: [Ingress] with one ingress rule. What happens to its egress traffic?
options: All egress traffic is allowed (the policy only controls ingress)
Egress is denied unless there is also an Egress policy type
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicy only controls the direction(s) listed in policyTypes. If only Ingress is listed, egress traffic is unaffected by this policy (defaults to allow). You need to explicitly add Egress to policyTypes and egress rules to restrict outbound traffic.

questions.q: Two `from` entries in the same ingress rule — how are they evaluated?
questions.explanation: Separate items in the `from` array are OR conditions — traffic is allowed if it matches any one of them. To require AND (e.g., a specific namespace AND a specific pod label), both selectors must be in the SAME list item (as fields of the same object).

questions.q: You apply a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy to a namespace. Pods can no longer resolve DNS hostnames. Why?
options: DNS resolution requires UDP/TCP port 53 egress to kube-system, which is now blocked
NetworkPolicy doesn't affect DNS because DNS uses UDP
questions.explanation: DNS resolution sends queries to kube-dns (in kube-system namespace) on port 53/UDP (and sometimes TCP). A default-deny-all policy blocks all egress including DNS. You must add an explicit egress rule allowing port 53 UDP/TCP to the kube-system namespace.

sections.title: Challenge: design a zero-trust policy set for a three-tier app
sections.goal: Design (write as YAML) a complete set of NetworkPolicies for a three-tier application with pods labeled: tier=frontend, tier=backend, tier=database. Apply the principle of least privilege: frontend accepts traffic from anywhere on port 80; frontend can call backend on port 8080; backend can call database on port 5432; database cannot initiate any outbound connection; all tiers can resolve DNS.
hints: You need at least 4 policies: one default-deny, and then whitelist policies for each tier
Start with default-deny-all on the namespace, then add specific allow rules
Remember DNS egress (port 53 UDP to kube-system) for all tiers that need it
Use separate NetworkPolicy objects per tier for clarity rather than one complex policy
success_criteria: A default-deny-all policy exists for the namespace
frontend policy allows ingress from anywhere on port 80
frontend policy allows egress only to backend on port 8080 (plus DNS)
backend policy allows ingress only from frontend on port 8080
backend policy allows egress only to database on port 5432 (plus DNS)
database policy allows ingress only from backend on port 5432
database policy has no egress rules (denies all egress)
